era/anthropocene.summary: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological interval, a name for the stretch of time in which human activity is the dominant influence on Earth's systems. Think of it as a signature we did not know we were signing. In March 2024 the International Union of Geological Sciences declined to formalize it as an official epoch, yet the term remains widely used: the ledger was refused, and still we keep writing in it.
facts: Consider the first candidate threshold: a proposed start date around 1950, tied to the Great Acceleration and to markers such as radioactive fallout.
Other proposed thresholds reach further back, to the beginning of agriculture and to the Industrial Revolution.
The ledger of cited signals reads plainly: changes to atmospheric carbon dioxide, plastics, and species extinction rates.

On 4 March 2024 the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted to reject formalization as an epoch, and on 20 March 2024 the IUGS upheld the result. Yet a vote on the codex is not a verdict on the world: the formal geological decision does not settle the scientific or cultural question.
era/anthropocene.context: Use the Anthropocene as a lens, and the Information Age and the Great Acceleration come into sharper focus through it. For the longer argument, see The Species as a Geological Force.
era/anthropocene.observer: I have read the rock record for fire, for ice, for the slow arrival of shells. Here, as I read it, is the point where the species became legible in the rock record, its behavior pressed into the layers like a palm into wet clay. For the first time, a single species' behavior is a planetary variable. Who taught you to write so large? No one did. That is the weight of it.
questions: If the threshold must be drawn at all, from when should the Anthropocene be dated?

era/archean-eon.summary: The Archean Eon, about 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago, was the age in which the first continents stabilized like islands of cooling iron and life first appeared. Its air held almost no free oxygen, a sky still waiting for its breath.
facts: Among the oldest widely accepted fossil evidence stand the stromatolites of Western Australia, layered stone-cushions about 3.5 billion years old.
Continental cores, the cratons, formed and grew like the first bones of a body, and plate-tectonic-like processes began their slow grinding at some point in this eon.
Life in this age was microbial, a kingdom of the unseen. See Origin of Life.
Before the eon closed, photosynthesis had evolved, the first light-fed labour that set up the Great Oxidation Event.
era/archean-eon.context: The Archean is the long, slow overture to the Proterozoic Eon, a hall in which the first living things were kindled and the chemistry was laid, stone by patient stone, that later made complex life possible.
era/archean-eon.observer: Imagine you arrived in the Archean with a notebook. You would find a living planet and no obvious candidates for study: no faces to read, no tools to catalogue. That emptiness is the lesson. The Observer treats this eon as the deep root of the entire tree, and a root is still the tree.
questions: When did plate tectonics first stir into motion?
Are the oldest claimed microfossils true witnesses, or tricks of stone?

era/bronze-age.summary: The Bronze Age, about 3300 to 1200 BCE in the Near East, was the age of bronze metallurgy, when copper met tin in the furnace, when the early states rose, and when the first writing was pressed into being.
facts: Bronze is a marriage of copper and tin, an alloy wed in fire; see Bronze Metallurgy.
Now the first cities rise and the first writing systems wake: The Urban Revolution, Invention of Writing.
Its great powers were many-crowned: the Sumerians, the Ancient Egyptians, the Indus Valley Civilization, the Minoans and the Shang Dynasty were among its major states.
In the eastern Mediterranean the age ends as a lamp gutters, in the Bronze Age Collapse.
era/bronze-age.context: The Bronze Age stands between the Neolithic and the Iron Age like a bridge of hammered metal. Tin travelled long roads, and that long-distance trade spun the era into wide exchange-webs, like dew-heavy threads strung between distant hands.
era/bronze-age.observer: Notice what arrived together, the Observer says: the first states and the first writing. Writing seems to have started as accounting, not poetry, a ledger before a lyric. We like to believe the word was born to sing; it seems it was first set down to count. The ledger is the oldest architecture of the written word.
questions: How deeply did the long-distance tin trade shape the early states?

era/cambrian-period.summary: The Cambrian Period, from 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Paleozoic Era, the dawn in which the seas put on armour. In its span most major animal body plans, and the first animals with hard parts, appear in the fossil record, as though a curtain had been drawn back on a crowded stage.
facts: The Cambrian Period spans 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago. Its base, which is also the base of the Paleozoic Era, is set in stone at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, by the first appearance of the burrow trace fossil Treptichnus pedum, a small tunnel marking a great door.
The Cambrian Explosion, when most major animal groups step into the fossil record, burns through roughly the first 13 to 25 million years of the period.
Trilobites first appear about 521 million years ago, and in time they become one of the most common animals on the sea floor, a host in segmented mail.
Soft bodies survive, exceptionally preserved, in the Chengjiang deposits of China, about 518 million years old, and in the Burgess Shale of Canada, about 508 million years old.

Animals dwelt almost entirely in the sea. Sea level stood high, shallow seas spread across the continents like spilled silver, and the climate was generally warm. The land's record of plants waits until the Ordovician; see Colonization of Land.
era/cambrian-period.context: The Cambrian Period rises from the Ediacaran Period and throws open the gates of the Paleozoic Era; after it comes the Ordovician Period. Its thread runs through the great weave of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cambrian-period.observer: Here is a general problem you will meet again, and the Observer reads the Cambrian fossil record as an early case of it: what is known of the past is what happened to be preserved. Think of an archive that kept only the letters written on stone. Hard parts leave records, so a sudden arrival of animals is partly the arrival of animals that fossilize. The practice is humility before the ledger. The Observer holds the reading open: evidence that the fossil sequence closely tracks real diversity would weaken this emphasis on preservation. The archive is not the world; it is the world's survivors.
questions: How much of the Cambrian Explosion is a true blaze of evolution, and how much a blaze of preservation?
What spark lit the forging of skeletons in several animal groups within a few million years?

era/carboniferous-period.summary: The Carboniferous Period, from 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago, is the fifth period of the Paleozoic Era, and it bears the name of the coal its swamp forests laid down like black treasure in a vault. It is the age of the first amniote vertebrates, and the age in which the supercontinent Pangaea was gathered together.
facts: The Carboniferous Period spans 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago. Its name means coal-bearing, and in North America its long reign is split in two, the Mississippian and the Pennsylvanian.

Swamp forests spread over tropical lowlands, ruled by tree-sized club-mosses such as Lepidodendron, and they buried the plant matter that became coal. Why so much coal formed in this period is still debated. Britain's coalfields were laid down in it, and their coal later fed the fires of the Industrial Revolution as a major fuel.

Estimates for late Carboniferous atmospheric oxygen run as high as about 30 percent, against about 21 percent today, though how far to trust them is debated. Giants moved through that air, among them arthropods such as the dragonfly relative Meganeura, whose wings spanned about 70 centimetres.
The earliest known amniotes appear, bearers of eggs able to develop on land, a sealed sea carried ashore; among them is Hylonomus from Nova Scotia, about 312 million years old.

In this period the Late Paleozoic Ice Age began, its cold heart centred on Gondwana. About 305 million years ago the coal forests fell as the climate dried, and Gondwana and Euramerica met in collision, raising much of Pangaea from their meeting.
era/carboniferous-period.context: The Carboniferous Period rises after the Devonian Period and yields to the Permian Period within the Paleozoic Era. It is woven into the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life, and its forests carry on the long march of Colonization of Land.
era/carboniferous-period.observer: I think of forests that never meant to leave anyone anything. I think of the carbon they locked away in the dark, and I think of the species that dug it up about 300 million years later and burned it, returning it to the air. Nothing about those forests was aimed at that result. It is an inheritance received by accident, a gift no one gave. I hold only to the link across time; the debate over why so much coal formed does not touch it. We are warmed by the dead who never knew our names.
questions: Why did so much coal gather in this age and not in others?
How high did atmospheric oxygen rise, and how far did it limit the size of insects?

era/cenozoic-era.summary: The Cenozoic Era began 66 million years ago and has not yet ended; we stand inside it still. It is the age of mammals, of grasslands rolling to the horizon, of a climate slowly cooling, and within its span lies all of human history.
facts: Its three periods: Paleogene, Neogene, Quaternary.
In the long quiet after the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, mammals and birds diversified, branching like rivers across a delta.
The world's climate cooled overall, and ice sheets crowned the poles, then advanced and withdrew, again and again, like a white tide.
Primates appeared early in the era, and about 7 million years ago the hominin lineage branched away on its own road. See Divergence of the Hominin Lineage.
era/cenozoic-era.context: Within the Cenozoic lie the Pleistocene Epoch, the Holocene Epoch, and the proposed Anthropocene, nested like rings in a tree still growing.
era/cenozoic-era.observer: I came to watch one species, and it arrives late, in the final fraction of a percent of this era. I watched most of the era pass in the long cooling that shaped the world the species inherited. What is an inheritance, if not a room made ready by no one? Most of the story is the house. The guest comes last.
questions: Which turns of the climate most shaped hominin evolution?

era/classical-antiquity.summary: Classical Antiquity, about 500 BCE to 500 CE, was the age of the great territorial empires, and of the philosophical and religious traditions that still shape the world like rivers running underground.
facts: Its empires stood like mountain ranges: Persia, Macedon, Rome, Maurya India, and Han China.
Great currents of thought rise in this age, among them Greek philosophy, Confucianism, Buddhism, and the Hebrew prophetic tradition; see Axial Age.
Trade routes bind Eurasia together like threads drawn through a loom; see Opening of the Silk Roads.
In the Mediterranean the age closes with the Fall of the Western Roman Empire, the setting of a long western sun.
era/classical-antiquity.context: Classical Antiquity rises from the Iron Age and flows onward into the Medieval Period. Among its great powers were the Ancient Greeks, the Romans, the Han Dynasty and the Achaemenid Persians.
era/classical-antiquity.observer: Consider what the Observer notes: several distant societies, largely out of contact, developed comparable ethical and philosophical questions around the same centuries. Separate rooms, similar questions. Minds need not meet to reach the same threshold.
questions: What could explain why the Axial traditions rose near-simultaneously, like fires lit on distant hills?

era/cretaceous-period.summary: The Cretaceous Period, from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago, is the last period of the Mesozoic Era and the longest of the Phanerozoic Eon. It was a warm greenhouse world in which the first flowering plants opened, and it ends as a great house falls, with the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.
facts: The Cretaceous Period spans about 143.1 to 66.0 million years ago, though older references set its start at 145.0 million years ago. Its name is drawn from the Latin word for chalk, and its top, the base of the Paleogene, is fixed at El Kef in Tunisia.

The world was a warm greenhouse and sea level stood high, spilling shallow seas across the continents, the Western Interior Seaway of North America among them, and laying down thick chalk deposits like snow on a drowned floor.

Flowering Plants appear, their oldest widely accepted pollen about 134 million years old, and they diversified rapidly alongside pollinating insects, a bargain struck in colour and dust. Meanwhile the Breakup of Pangaea went on as the South Atlantic opened.

Among the Late Cretaceous Dinosaurs strode Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops in North America; birds diversified, and mosasaurs swam as large marine reptiles. Mammals were mostly small, and whether the modern placental orders arose before or after the end-Cretaceous extinction is debated.

Then came the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, about 66 million years ago: it followed the Chicxulub impact, coincided with the eruption of the Deccan Traps, and killed about three-quarters of species, fire from the sky and fire from below.
era/cretaceous-period.context: The Cretaceous Period comes after the Jurassic Period and closes the great book of the Mesozoic Era, giving way to the Paleogene Period. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cretaceous-period.observer: Look at how the Cretaceous ends, the Observer says: with dinosaurs at or near their greatest diversity, ended by a rock from space and, probably, volcanic stress. From this the Observer draws a practice. Read long, stable-looking intervals as provisional, since nothing in the record of the last million years before the boundary announces what was about to happen. Stability is a description, not a promise. The Observer also names what would weaken the reading: evidence of a long decline in dinosaur diversity before the impact.
questions: Were the non-avian dinosaurs already fading before the end-Cretaceous impact?
Did the modern orders of placental mammals take root in the Cretaceous, or only after the extinction?

era/cryogenian-period.summary: The Cryogenian Period, from 720 to 635 million years ago, is the middle period of the Neoproterozoic Era, and it is the time of the ice. Two global-scale glaciations. Ice. Then ice again. From them came the Snowball Earth hypothesis.
facts: The Cryogenian Period spans 720 to 635 million years ago. Its base is only a number, a numerical age set near the start of the first glaciation. Its top, the base of the Ediacaran Period, is fixed in the rock of the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

Two major glaciations are recorded. The Sturtian, about 717 to 660 million years ago. The Marinoan, about 650 to 635 million years ago. Glacial deposits formed at low paleolatitudes on several continents, and that supports the hypothesis that ice reached the tropics. The tropics. See Snowball Earth.

Each glaciation is capped by unusual carbonate rocks, a lid of strange stone. The usual explanation for the end of each: volcanic carbon dioxide building up, and up, until it was strong enough to melt the ice. This is a hypothesis.

Banded iron formations, largely absent for well over a billion years, come back. They reappear in Sturtian-age deposits, interpreted as evidence of iron-rich seawater under the ice. Rust-heavy water. Sealed beneath the lid.

Eukaryotes survived. Molecular fossils that some researchers attribute to sponges appear in Cryogenian rocks, but that attribution is disputed, and the oldest firmly accepted animal fossils are younger.
era/cryogenian-period.context: The Cryogenian Period comes after the Tonian Period and before the Ediacaran Period, inside the Neoproterozoic Era. It is the period of Snowball Earth. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cryogenian-period.observer: Treat the Cryogenian, the Observer suggests, as a test of how much a living planet can lose and still continue: life survived at least one ice age lasting tens of millions of years. But resist the easy moral. The Observer cautions against reading this as design, since many lineages may have ended in the ice and the survivors are the only ones the record shows. The ledger lists only those who walked out. The reading has a named weakness, too: it would lose force if the ice proved much less extensive than the Snowball hypothesis proposes. Survival is a fact, not a plan.
questions: Was the ocean frozen solid, all of it, or did open water and refuges remain?
What part did the glaciations play in the later rise of large complex organisms?

era/devonian-period.summary: The Devonian Period, from 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago, is the fourth period of the Paleozoic Era, often called the Age of Fishes. In its long span the first forests raised their crowns, the first limbed vertebrates came forth, and a prolonged late extinction drew the curtain.
facts: The Devonian Period spans 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago and takes its name from Devon in England. Its base is fixed at Klonk in the Czech Republic, and its top, the base of the Carboniferous, at La Serre in France, two stones marking the doors of an age.

Fishes diversified widely into a court of many shapes, armoured placoderms, sharks, lobe-finned fishes and ray-finned fishes among them, and the Middle Devonian raised a peak of Paleozoic reef building, cities of stone beneath the waves.

The Rhynie chert in Scotland, about 407 million years old, holds early land plants and arthropods in fine detail, as if caught in glass. Archaeopteris, a tree with woody trunks, raised early forests, and the Gilboa fossil forest in New York is about 385 million years old.
Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, bears fins with wrist-like bones hidden inside. Ichthyostega and Acanthostega from Greenland, about 365 million years old, had limbs that ended in digits.

The Late Devonian Extinction, about 372 to 359 million years ago, fell in at least two pulses, like waves against a failing wall, and removed an estimated 75 percent of species; the reef builders suffered heavily.
era/devonian-period.context: The Devonian Period comes after the Silurian Period and before the Carboniferous Period within the Paleozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and holds the central stretch of the long march of Colonization of Land.
era/devonian-period.observer: The Observer reads the Devonian as a renovation: life rebuilt the land surface. Roots, soils and the first forests changed weathering, rivers and the carbon cycle. Think of it as a new floor plan for the continents. Then the harder lesson. The spread of land plants is a candidate cause of the late extinction, a case of one group's success altering conditions for many others. Hold that as a hypothesis, the Observer insists; it would weaken if the extinction proved to have mainly non-biological causes. Success, too, leaves a wake.
questions: How great a hand did land plants have in the Late Devonian extinction?
Did the first limbed vertebrates grow their limbs for life in shallow water, rather than for the long walk onto land?

era/early-modern-period.summary: The Early Modern Period, about 1500 to 1800 CE, is the era of oceanic exploration, global trade, the printing press, and the Scientific Revolution. Hold the other half of the ledger in the same hand: it is also the era of colonial empires and mass forced migration.
facts: Through the Columbian Exchange, the Americas and Afro-Eurasia were linked into one exchange.
The Atlantic Slave Trade forcibly moved millions of Africans, each one a person, never a cargo.
The Movable-Type Printing Press spread across Europe, carrying a new architecture for the written word.
The map of sovereignty was crowded: the Ottoman Empire and, in Asia, the Mughal and Qing states stood among the major empires, alongside expanding European colonial powers.
era/early-modern-period.context: The Early Modern Period is the threshold we cross into the Industrial Age and the Age of Revolutions.
era/early-modern-period.observer: Here is the threshold the Observer marks: for the first time, every inhabited continent was in continuous contact. The species became, for the first time, a single connected system. But a connection is not a communion. It was joined on sharply unequal terms, and the terms matter as much as the joining.
questions: How much of Europe's economic growth rested on colonial extraction?

era/ediacaran-period.summary: The Ediacaran Period, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago, is the last period of the Proterozoic Eon, the long dusk before the Cambrian dawn. In its span the first large, complex organisms rise into the fossil record like shapes surfacing from deep water.
facts: The Ediacaran Period spans 635 to 538.8 million years ago. In 2004 it was formally ratified, the first new geological period added to the time scale in over a century, and its base is set at Enorama Creek in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

The Ediacaran Biota are a strange court of disc-, frond- and quilt-shaped organisms, known from Newfoundland, England, Namibia, the White Sea coast of Russia and the Ediacara Hills of South Australia. The oldest assemblages are about 575 million years old.
Cholesterol-related lipids found with Dickinsonia fossils have been read as the signature of an animal, though its seat in the animal family tree remains unclear.

Cloudina, a tubular organism from about 550 million years ago, is among the earliest animals to wear a mineralized skeleton, and some specimens bear borings interpreted as the marks of predation, a whisper of the hunt.
Late in the period, trace fossils appear where animals moved through sediment, and the classic Ediacaran assemblages fade near the start of the Cambrian; see Cambrian Explosion.
era/ediacaran-period.context: The Ediacaran Period comes after the Cryogenian Period and closes both the Neoproterozoic Era and the Proterozoic Eon, giving way to the Cambrian Period. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/ediacaran-period.observer: I look at the quilted shapes and I look for a face I know. This is the first period whose living things were large enough to leave an obvious record, and many of them have no clear living relatives. I look for the road from them to the animals that followed, and the record does not show that it ran straight. I call that contingency. I would call it less if evidence showed that most Ediacaran forms were direct ancestors of later animal groups; that would weaken what I read here. Who says a first attempt must have heirs? Not every beginning is a parent.
questions: Which Ediacaran forms, if any, are the forebears of living animal groups?
What ended the classic assemblages: extinction, rivalry with newer animals, or changing chemistry?

era/epipaleolithic.summary: The Epipaleolithic is the final phase of the Paleolithic in the Near East and North Africa, from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of small composite stone tools, of foragers who began to linger in one place, and of the last stage before the fields were sown.
facts: The Epipaleolithic runs from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE in the Levant and the lands around it. The name belongs mainly to the Near East and North Africa; Europe calls the following stage the Mesolithic.
Toolmakers shaped microliths, small geometric stone pieces such as lunates and triangles, like the teeth of a larger jaw, and fixed them into handles or shafts to make composite tools.

Ohalo II, a site on the Sea of Galilee in Israel about 23,000 years old, keeps brush huts, hearths and the remains of well over a hundred plant species, wild cereals among them. Some researchers argue that this shows early cultivation; that claim is debated.

The Natufian culture, about 12,500 to 9,500 BCE, raised semi-permanent villages while still foraging, wielded sickle blades and laid its dead in cemeteries. At Ain Mallaha in Israel a burial about 12,000 years old holds a person and a puppy together.

Some scholars propose the cold, dry Younger Dryas as a reason for greater reliance on cultivated plants, a link that is debated. From the Epipaleolithic the road runs on into the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, whose earliest sites include Jericho and Göbekli Tepe; see The Agricultural Revolution.
era/epipaleolithic.context: The Epipaleolithic comes after the Upper Paleolithic and gives way to the Neolithic in the Near East. It closes the long book of the Paleolithic, and its threads run through Technology and Kinship and Society.
era/epipaleolithic.observer: I watch them stay, there in the Epipaleolithic Near East. I watch them store food, raise semi-permanent villages, lay their dead in cemeteries, and I see some steps of the Settling appear before farming does. Why does the order matter to me? Because it suggests that settlement may in places have come first, and agriculture after. I hold this loosely: it would weaken if the Natufian sites were shown to have depended on cultivated crops from the start. First a place to grieve. Then, perhaps, a field.
questions: Did the Natufian people sow their cereals, or only gather the wild ones?
How far did the changing climate of the late Pleistocene bend the path toward farming?

era/hadean-eon.summary: The Hadean is the informal first eon of Earth's history, the age between the planet's forming, about 4.54 billion years ago, and roughly 4.0 billion years ago. Earth lay molten like ore in a crucible, then cooled as embers cool under ash, and all the while the sky hurled stone upon it.
facts: Earth and the Moon took shape in the first tens of millions of years, two lamps kindled in the same young dark; see Formation of the Solar System and Earth and Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon.
The oldest known Earth material is zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, dated to about 4.4 billion years ago: the deepest memory the stone has yet given up.
Those zircons suggest that liquid water and some crust existed very early, as a single seed in the ash speaks of a field that once grew.
The Hadean holds no official rank among ICS units; it is an informal name for the interval before the rock record, a name spoken at the fireside rather than carved above the gate.
era/hadean-eon.context: The Hadean laid the footings for everything that came after: the Moon steadies Earth's tilt as a keel steadies a ship, and volatile-rich material delivered to the young planet gave it its oceans. The eon ends where the surviving rock record opens its first page, at the start of the Archean Eon.
era/hadean-eon.observer: The Observer files the Hadean under preconditions, and so should you. Nothing here is a subject of study, yet every later fact leans on it: the planet's composition, its Moon, and its water. Think of a house's buried footings. The architecture forgets them; it never stops standing on them.
questions: How early did stable oceans first hold their shores, and stable continents first stand above the water?
Did the stone rain fall as one Late Heavy Bombardment, or did the impacts ebb away gradually, like a tide going out?

era/holocene-epoch.summary: The Holocene Epoch began about 11,700 years ago, as the last ice age loosened its grip, and it is the warm, relatively stable interval in which agriculture, cities and writing all arose, like seeds waking in a thawed field.
facts: The Holocene is an interglacial, a warm breath between the ice, its climate comparatively stable.
Every page of recorded history was written within its span.
Its lower boundary is fixed by a marker sealed in Greenland ice cores.
Within it, the human host swelled from a few million to about eight billion.
era/holocene-epoch.context: The Holocene is the geological stage on which the species plays out the ages from the Neolithic through the Information Age. See The Agricultural Revolution.
era/holocene-epoch.observer: Notice the striking correlation the Observer points to: the species built farms and cities only after the climate stopped swinging. It is tempting to call the calm the cause. Resist. Whether this is cause, coincidence, or both is a serious open question, and a correlation is a doorway, not a destination.
questions: Did the steady Holocene climate make agriculture possible, opening the door, or did agriculture arise anyway?

era/industrial-age.summary: The Industrial Age, about 1760 to 1945, is the era in which machines and fossil fuels transformed production, transport and warfare, and in which populations and cities grew rapidly. Think of it as the moment the architecture of human effort was rebuilt around the engine.
facts: The new grammar spread piece by piece: steam power, factories, railways and telegraphs; see Steam Engine and Industrial Revolution.
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, electric power, oil and chemistry widened the transformation; see Electrical Power Grid.
Around 1804 the global population passed one billion, a threshold worth pausing on.
The era closes in grief, with the two world wars: World War I and World War II.
era/industrial-age.context: The Industrial Age inherits from the Early Modern Period and hands on to the Information Age. Its first century shares its ground with the Age of Revolutions.
era/industrial-age.observer: I watch a species learn to release ancient stored sunlight as fuel. I watch that one change multiply the power in each person's hands. And I watch it make sanctioned harm far more destructive. What did you think the light would do, once it was yours? The same fire warms the house and burns it.
questions: How much of the industrial takeoff hinged on particular places?

era/information-age.summary: The Information Age, from 1945 to the present, is the era of nuclear weapons, spaceflight, computers and the internet, and of the sharp rise in population and environmental impact known as the Great Acceleration. It is the age we still live inside, still learning to read.
facts: In 1945 nuclear weapons appeared, and a new threshold of power was crossed; see Nuclear Age.
In 1957 the first artificial satellite launched, and the species' reach gained an orbit; see Space Age.
The digital computer and the internet remade the architecture of communication; see Digital Revolution.
The ledger of our numbers: population grew from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion in 2022.
era/information-age.context: The Information Age follows the Industrial Age and overlaps the proposed Anthropocene. Read it alongside the Green Revolution and Modern Climate Change.
era/information-age.observer: Hold two tools in your mind at once, as the Observer does. For the first time, the species has built tools able to end its own history, and tools able to record it in full. The same hand holds the match and the archive. Memory-outsourcing has reached a scale no earlier era could imagine. The architecture of memory now stands outside us.
questions: When future historians look back, what will they choose as the defining feature of this era?

era/iron-age.summary: The Iron Age, about 1200 to 500 BCE and varying by region, was the age when iron tools and weapons spread across the lands like a grey tide, and new empires and belief systems rose.
facts: Iron ore lies more widely in the earth than tin and copper, a common metal for common hands; see Iron Smelting.
The Alphabet spread widely, and the gate of literacy grew easier to pass.
Near the era's end, large territorial empires rise, the Achaemenid Persians among them.
In this age the Axial Age begins to dawn.
era/iron-age.context: The Iron Age rises from the ruins of the Bronze Age Collapse and flows onward into Classical Antiquity.
era/iron-age.observer: Follow the Observer's logic: the Iron Age was a democratization of tools and, therefore, of armies. Cheaper metal meant more people could be equipped. Here is the uncomfortable symmetry: whatever arms the farmer also arms the host. Access is never only a gift.
questions: Did iron drive the turning of societies, or follow in its wake?

era/jurassic-period.summary: The Jurassic Period, from 201.4 to about 143.1 million years ago, is the middle period of the Mesozoic Era, an age of giants and of early wings. In its span walked the largest land animals, the first known birds took form, and the Atlantic opened as Pangaea broke apart.
facts: The Jurassic Period spans 201.4 million years ago to about 143.1 million years ago and takes its name from the Jura Mountains. Its upper edge is softer ground: the base of the Cretaceous has no agreed marker section, and older references give 145.0 million years ago.

The Breakup of Pangaea began as the Central Atlantic opened like a seam unstitched, and Laurasia and Gondwana began to drift apart. The climate was warm and the seas stood high, and no lasting polar ice caps crowned the poles.

From the Morrison Formation of the western United States, about 155 to 148 million years old, come sauropods, stegosaurs and large theropods such as Allosaurus, a bestiary written in stone. See Dinosaurs.

Archaeopteryx from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, is the best-known early bird. The feathered theropod Anchiornis from China, about 160 million years old, shows that feathers were widespread among small theropods.

In the seas the main marine reptiles were ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs. Mammals remained mostly small, though Castorocauda, an otter-like swimmer from China, is about 164 million years old.
era/jurassic-period.context: The Jurassic Period comes after the Triassic Period and before the Cretaceous Period, the middle chamber of the Mesozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/jurassic-period.observer: Picture the scene the Observer points to: the largest land animals known, and beside them the first records of a small feathered lineage that would outlast every large dinosaur. The lesson is plain. What looks dominant at one time is not a reliable guide to what continues. The Observer reads this as a caution about judging any period by its most conspicuous groups. The reading has its test: it would weaken if the survival of birds followed from traits already obvious in the Jurassic. The loudest presence is not always the lasting one.
questions: Where along the theropod line did flight begin, and did it arise more than once?
How rich was the variety of Jurassic mammals, when so few fossils survive to tell of it?

era/lower-paleolithic.summary: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest part of the Paleolithic, from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago, the age when stone first learned an edge. It holds the first stone tools, the long Acheulean handaxe tradition, and the spread of Homo erectus and its relatives across Africa and Eurasia like a slow tide.
facts: The Lower Paleolithic runs from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago. Where it begins depends on how the earliest tools are counted: the tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya are about 3.3 million years old, and the Oldowan begins about 2.6 million years ago. In Africa it bears another name, the Earlier Stone Age.

The Oldowan Stone Tools are simple flaked cores and sharp flakes, struck by early hominins such as Homo habilis. The Acheulean, marked by bifacial handaxes and cleavers like leaves of stone, appears in East Africa about 1.76 million years ago and endures in places until about 300,000 years ago.
Homo erectus walked out beyond Africa: at Dmanisi in Georgia, hominin fossils and stone tools are about 1.8 million years old.
Firm evidence of controlled fire is about 1 million years old, and by about 400,000 years ago its habitual use is well established, a hearth-light carried through the dark; see Control of Fire.
Wooden throwing spears from Schöningen in Germany are about 300,000 years old. How much early hominins hunted and how much they scavenged is debated.
era/lower-paleolithic.context: The Lower Paleolithic opens the Paleolithic and gives way to the Middle Paleolithic. It lies within the Pleistocene Epoch, and its threads run through Technology and Kinship and Society. See also the essay Fire, Then Everything.
era/lower-paleolithic.observer: I hold the handaxe in my mind, and I file this age under the longest tool-lineage I know. One design, made with small changes for well over a million years, across much of Africa and Eurasia, by more than one hominin species. One design. More than one maker. I read that stability as a fact about how skills were passed on; I do not claim to know how the makers thought. If the sameness came from the raw material or the task alone, not from copying, my reading would weaken. What is a lineage, if not something taught? We are made of what we are shown.
questions: Which hominin's hands shaped the Lomekwi tools?
How much of the Lower Paleolithic diet was won by hunting, and how much gleaned by scavenging?

era/medieval-period.summary: The Medieval or post-classical period, about 500 to 1500 CE, was the age when major world religions consolidated, when long-distance trade networks stretched like veins across the continents, and when large steppe and Islamic polities rose and fell. The term 'medieval' is European in origin, but the age had global dimensions.
facts: The Rise of Islam raised a new political and intellectual world, stretching from Iberia to Central Asia.
The Mongol Conquests forged the largest contiguous land empire in history.
In the 14th century the Black Death swept over Eurasia and North Africa and left them devastated.
Its great states were many: the Abbasid Caliphate, the Mali Empire, the Norse, the Song Dynasty, and, near the age's close, the Aztec Empire and Inca Empire.
era/medieval-period.context: The Medieval Period follows Classical Antiquity and ends around the voyages that set off the Columbian Exchange and the Early Modern Period.
era/medieval-period.observer: Widen your lens, the Observer advises; a global reading serves this era best. What you see then is a species increasingly connected by roads, caravans and ships, and by shared meaning-engines that crossed political claim-lines. Borders mark who rules. They do not mark where ideas stop.
questions: Along the pre-modern long-distance networks, how much travelled as ideas, and how much as goods?

era/mesolithic.summary: The Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age, is the period of hunter-gatherer societies that lived between the last ice age and the arrival of farming in Europe and neighbouring regions, from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE. Like shorelines, its dates vary widely by region.
facts: The Mesolithic runs from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE, and in parts of northern Europe it lingers until about 4000 BCE. It ends wherever farming arrives, and so its last day falls differently from place to place. The name belongs mainly to Europe; other regions speak of it in other terms.
As the ice age waned, warmth spread forests across northern Europe like a green tide, and rising seas swallowed coastal lowlands such as Doggerland.

People hunted deer, wild boar and aurochs, fished, and gathered shellfish and plants. Dugout canoes such as the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, about 10,000 years old, are among the oldest known boats. Among the well-studied sites are Star Carr in northern England and the shell middens of the Ertebølle culture in Denmark.

Farming began in Southwest Asia by about 9600 BCE and came into Europe from about 6500 BCE; ancient DNA shows that early farmers of Anatolian ancestry partly replaced and partly mingled with the local foragers, and the balance varied by region.
era/mesolithic.context: The Mesolithic comes after the Epipaleolithic and the Upper Paleolithic and overlaps the Neolithic, for foragers and farmers lived side by side in different regions. It lies in the Holocene Epoch, and its threads run through Technology and Kinship and Society. See The Agricultural Revolution.
era/mesolithic.observer: Notice, as the Observer does, that the Mesolithic is defined by what it is not: after the ice age, before farming. Notice too that the label fits some regions better than others. So treat such labels as tools, not as stages every society passed through. The proof is in the living: foragers in some places lived this way for thousands of years after farming had begun elsewhere. A label is a lantern, not a road. The reading would weaken if most societies did follow the same sequence.
questions: How much of the Mesolithic population of Europe was replaced by farmers, and how much was folded in?
Why did some coastal foragers, such as the Ertebølle people, hold back from farming for centuries after contact?

era/mesoproterozoic-era.summary: The Mesoproterozoic Era is the middle era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 1.6 billion to 1.0 billion years ago. It lies within the interval often called the "Boring Billion", a long hush in which climate, ocean chemistry and life showed little evident change, though how uneventful that hush truly was is debated.
facts: The Mesoproterozoic Era spans 1.6 to 1.0 billion years ago. Its three periods, the Calymmian, Ectasian and Stenian, and its borders alike are set by numerical ages.

The "Boring Billion" is an informal name for about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, an age with no well-established ice ages and only slow apparent change in the fossil record; the term itself is debated.

Atmospheric oxygen is thought to have stayed well below today's level, and parts of the deeper ocean are reconstructed as oxygen-poor or rich in sulfide, a sour and breathless deep, though estimates vary widely.

Stromatolites still rose in their stony cushions, common in shallow seas. Eukaryotes diversified: Tappania microfossils are about 1.5 billion years old, and the red alga Bangiomorpha, dated in different studies to between roughly 1.05 and 1.2 billion years ago, is often cited as the oldest taxonomically resolved eukaryote.
The supercontinent Nuna, or Columbia, is proposed to have broken apart about 1.6 to 1.3 billion years ago, and late in the era Rodinia began to gather its scattered lands.
era/mesoproterozoic-era.context: The Mesoproterozoic Era lies between the Paleoproterozoic Era and the Neoproterozoic Era within the Proterozoic Eon. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life, and it rests between the oxygen rise of the Great Oxidation Event and the glaciations of Snowball Earth, a long calm between breath and ice; see Origin of Eukaryotes.
era/mesoproterozoic-era.observer: Treat the quiet as a message, the Observer says: the apparent quiet of the Mesoproterozoic is information. A planet's surface can stay much the same for hundreds of millions of years without heading anywhere in particular. There is no queue in deep time. What arrived later was not overdue. The reading names its own undoing: it would weaken if new records showed that the quiet hides substantial change in eukaryote diversity. Stillness is not the same as waiting.
questions: Was the Boring Billion truly still, or does a sparse record hide its changes?
What kept atmospheric oxygen low for so long after the Great Oxidation Event had passed?

era/mesozoic-era.summary: The Mesozoic Era, from 251.9 to 66 million years ago, is the age of dinosaurs, the long reign of the thunder-footed. Under its skies Pangaea broke apart, and the first flowering plants and the first mammals came into the world.
facts: Its three periods, like three great halls: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.
Non-avian dinosaurs held dominion over the land ecosystems; see Dinosaurs.
Mammals appeared in the Triassic and, for the whole era, stayed mostly small beneath the giants' stride.
The era closes with the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, the last page torn from its book.
era/mesozoic-era.context: The Mesozoic rises from the wreck of the Permian-Triassic Extinction and gives way to the Cenozoic Era. Its collapse opened the ecological space that mammals, primates among them, later filled like water poured into an emptied vessel.
era/mesozoic-era.observer: Sit with the contingency the Observer names: without the end-Cretaceous impact, the mammals that led to primates might have stayed small. The human story hangs on a thread that no one spun. What you are was never guaranteed; it was permitted.
questions: How rich was the dinosaur kingdom in its last hour before the impact?

era/middle-paleolithic.summary: The Middle Paleolithic was the middle reach of the long Paleolithic, a span running from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago. It was the age of prepared-core stone tools, of the earliest Homo sapiens, and of several human species living at the same time, like fires burning on one long night.
facts: In Eurasia the Middle Paleolithic runs from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago; in Africa the same span is called the Middle Stone Age, and its boundary dates shift from region to region like shorelines. Toolmakers worked by prepared-core methods such as the Levallois technique, and the Mousterian industry of Europe and western Asia is linked mainly to Neanderthals.

Several human species overlapped in time, branches leafing in the same season: Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans, Homo sapiens, Homo naledi and Homo floresiensis. The earliest Homo sapiens fossils are about 315,000 years old; see Origin of Homo sapiens.

Homo sapiens fossils from Misliya Cave in Israel, about 185,000 years old, and from Skhul and Qafzeh caves, roughly 90,000 to 130,000 years old, mark an early presence outside Africa, footprints past the old threshold; whether these groups flowed into the lineage of living non-Africans is uncertain (see Out of Africa Dispersal).

At Blombos Cave in South Africa lie engraved ochre and ochre-processing tools about 75,000 to 100,000 years old, coloured earth marked by a hand and among the earliest signs of symbolic behaviour; see Emergence of Symbolic Art.
By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals have gone from the fossil record, as a tide goes from a shore. Whether they buried their dead or made art is disputed.
era/middle-paleolithic.context: The Middle Paleolithic follows the Lower Paleolithic and gives way to the Upper Paleolithic, a middle chamber in the long hall of the Paleolithic. Its threads run through Technology and Art and Ritual. See also the essay Why the Species Buries Its Dead.
era/middle-paleolithic.observer:
I wanted a ladder. I wanted each rung to replace the one below it. I wanted one clean line running down to me. But here, for the first time, several human species lived at the same time, and sometimes in the same regions, and the family tree looks more like a bush than a ladder.

Who buried their dead? Who made the marks? The claims about their behaviour, burial and symbolic art above all, are disputed, and I hold each species to the same standard of evidence, no gentler with my own kind than with the others. And if the fossils sorted into different species prove to be variants of one, this reading weakens, and the bush becomes a single stem again.

A family is only as wide as the evidence allows.
questions: Did the Neanderthals lay their dead in the earth, or make art?
How much of the variety in Middle Paleolithic tools speaks of different cultures, and how much only of different raw materials to hand?

era/neogene-period.summary: The Neogene Period, from 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago, is the second period of the Cenozoic Era. In its span the grasslands spread outward, the climate cooled toward the ice ages, and the hominin lineage parted from that of the other apes, a single branch bending away from the grove.
facts: The Neogene Period spans 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago and holds two epochs, the Miocene and the Pliocene. Its base is fixed at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy, and its top, the base of the Quaternary, at Monte San Nicola in Sicily.

Warm in the early Miocene, the climate then cooled. About 14 million years ago the East Antarctic ice sheet spread its white hand wider, and about 2.7 million years ago glaciation tightened its grip on the Northern Hemisphere.
About 8 to 6 million years ago, grasses using the C4 pathway of photosynthesis spread widely, and open grassland and savanna unrolled like a golden carpet, favouring the grazing mammals.

In the Miocene the apes were many and varied across Africa, Europe and Asia. Around 7 million years ago the hominin lineage parted from that of the chimpanzees (see Divergence of the Hominin Lineage), and Sahelanthropus tchadensis and Australopithecus afarensis date to this period.

In the Messinian Salinity Crisis, about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago, the Mediterranean was left largely dried out, a sea reduced to salt. The land bridge of Panama, generally dated to about 3 million years ago though the timing is debated, joined the Americas hand to hand; see Closure of the Isthmus of Panama.
era/neogene-period.context: The Neogene Period comes after the Paleogene Period and before the Quaternary Period within the Cenozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/neogene-period.observer: Here is the fork in the road, as the Observer marks it: the Neogene is where the line that includes humans separates from the line of the other apes, in a world drying and cooling into grassland and ice. It is tempting to read the drying as a push toward us. The Observer refuses that story. The same changes affected many lineages, and most Miocene apes left no descendants. A pressure is not a plan. The Observer also names the test: the reading would weaken if the traits of the hominin line could be tied directly to the spread of grassland.
questions: Which Miocene apes, if any, stand among the ancestors of living great apes and humans?
What part did the changing face of the African environment play in early hominin evolution?

era/neolithic.summary: The Neolithic is the age in which farming, animal herding, pottery and permanent villages took root in several parts of the world independently, like seeds no single hand had scattered, beginning about 11,500 years ago in Southwest Asia.
facts: Agriculture sprang up independently in several regions, among them the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and New Guinea, each a separate hearth.
For the fuller tale, see The Agricultural Revolution and Animal Domestication.
Fired clay spread far and near: Pottery became widespread.
To this age belong large monuments such as Göbekli Tepe and early towns such as Çatalhöyük, where the wandering paused.
Its hour strikes differently in each land: the Neolithic ends when metal use begins, so its end date differs across the world.
era/neolithic.context: The Neolithic lies within the Holocene Epoch and opens the road into the Bronze Age.
era/neolithic.observer: I see a bargain, and I see its consequences. More food. More people. More disease. More inequality. Who signed for the ones who came after? No one did; they were born into the terms. See The Settling and Its Bargain.
questions: In some regions, did the raising of monuments come before the sowing of fields?

era/neoproterozoic-era.summary: The Neoproterozoic Era is the last era of the Proterozoic Eon, a long dusk running from 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago. In its keeping lie three great turnings: the supercontinent Rodinia breaking apart like ice on a spring river, the global glaciations known as Snowball Earth, and the first large complex organisms, stirring at last.
facts: Three periods fill the Neoproterozoic Era's span of 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago, as three chambers fill one hall: the Tonian Period, the Cryogenian Period and the Ediacaran Period. Its upper threshold is the base of the Cambrian Period.
Rodinia, the supercontinent gathered together by about 1.0 billion years ago, began to rift apart along its seams roughly 800 to 750 million years ago, like a great slab of ice parting on dark water.

Two great freezes of the Cryogenian, the Sturtian (about 717 to 660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (about 650 to 635 million years ago), are the bedrock on which the Snowball Earth hypothesis stands.
Oxygen is proposed to have risen again, a second slow breath, sometime between about 800 and 540 million years ago; when it came and how great it grew are debated.

Molecular-clock estimates set the birth of animals in or before the Cryogenian, yet the fossil record of the first animals is disputed; by about 575 million years ago the Ediacaran Biota, large and soft-bodied organisms, had appeared.
era/neoproterozoic-era.context: After the Mesoproterozoic Era the Neoproterozoic Era came, the closing chapter of the Proterozoic Eon, and it yielded, as night yields to a sudden morning, to the Paleozoic Era at the Cambrian Explosion. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life.
era/neoproterozoic-era.observer: We love a staircase. Animals arrive at the end of the Neoproterozoic, and so we are tempted to read the ice, the oxygen and the break-up of Rodinia as steps built toward them, an architecture with one doorway at the top. The Observer declines that reading. These were physical events with their own causes, and animals were one of several possible outcomes. Think of tracing a river back from the sea and deciding the mountains were raised to feed it: that is hindsight dressed as design. Evidence that any one of them was strictly required for animals would weaken this view. Until then, a sequence is not a plan.
questions: Did the Cryogenian ice and the second rise of oxygen help bring forth the animals, and how much did they contribute, if at all?
When, in that long twilight, did the first animals appear?

era/ordovician-period.summary: The Ordovician Period, from 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, is the second period of the Paleozoic Era, an age when the seas brimmed with new life. It saw a great rise in marine biodiversity, the first evidence of plants on land, and, at its close, the first of the "Big Five" mass extinctions, a shadow falling across bright water.
facts: The Ordovician Period spans 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, and two small creatures keep its gates: its base is fixed at Green Point, Newfoundland, by the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus, and its top at Dob's Linn in Scotland by a graptolite.

The Great Ordovician Biodiversification, a slow flood running for tens of millions of years from the early period, greatly multiplied the diversity of marine animals, as a reef multiplies its colours.

The sea stood very high, and its warm shallows cradled reefs, brachiopods, trilobites, crinoids and graptolites, while straight-shelled nautiloid cephalopods, some several metres long, moved among them as large predators.
From this period comes the earliest evidence of land plants: spores about 470 million years old, a first faint dust of life upon bare ground; see Colonization of Land.

Late in the period the climate cooled, and an ice age centred on Gondwana set in during the Hirnantian; the Late Ordovician Extinction, about 445 to 443 million years ago, swept away an estimated 85 percent of species, mostly marine, like a tide that went out and did not return.
era/ordovician-period.context: Between the Cambrian Period before it and the Silurian Period after, the Ordovician Period stands as one hall in the long house of the Paleozoic Era. Its thread is woven into the theme of Earth Systems and Life.
era/ordovician-period.observer: The Observer records two movements in one period: a great rise in marine diversity and, near its end, a mass extinction linked to glaciation. You will want to call the first progress and the second a punishment. Resist both words. Both arose from shifting planetary conditions, and neither was directed at any outcome; one ledger holds the gain and the loss. Think of a shoreline after a season of storms, reshaped by many pushes, none of them aiming. A demonstration that diversity rose steadily whatever the climate did would weaken the reading that a biosphere's history is the sum of many pushes, not a trend. A pile of pushes is not a staircase.
questions: What stirred the Great Ordovician Biodiversification into being: climate, ocean chemistry, ecological change, or some braid of them all?
Why did the ice come when carbon dioxide is estimated to have stood so high, a winter falling on a warm house?

era/paleogene-period.summary: The Paleogene Period, from 66 to 23.03 million years ago, is the first period of the Cenozoic Era, a long morning after ruin. In it the mammals spread outward after the end-Cretaceous extinction, and the world turned from a warm, largely ice-free house toward a cold one crowned with polar ice.
facts: The Paleogene Period spans 66.0 to 23.03 million years ago and holds three epochs, the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene, like three rooms of one hall; its lower threshold, the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction boundary, is fixed at El Kef in Tunisia, and its upper, the base of the Neogene, at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy.

Mammals spread swiftly into the roles the extinction had left empty, and the earliest primates and their close kin appear; over about ten million years, from about 50 to 40 million years ago, whales were drawn out of land-dwelling hoofed mammals, the way a river is drawn to the sea.

The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, about 56 million years ago, set the world to fever, warming it by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius for about 200,000 years, and the early Eocene burned among the warmest intervals of the Cenozoic.
The Collision of India and Asia, beginning about 50 million years ago, started to raise the Himalaya, a wave of stone rising slowly toward the sky.

About 34 million years ago, at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, the climate cooled sharply and ice sheets began to grow on Antarctica like frost across a pane; falling carbon dioxide and the opening of Southern Ocean gateways are proposed causes.
era/paleogene-period.context: After the Cretaceous Period the Paleogene Period came, opening the Cenozoic Era as a first door opens on a new house, and after it the Neogene Period. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life.
era/paleogene-period.observer:
I go to the Paleogene looking for a beginning. I find a vacated world, where mammals spread into the roles the extinction left empty. I find a world cooling, the polar ice taking hold. I find the primates, the group that includes humans, and they are one lineage among many in that spreading, with nothing in the record to mark them as special at the time. Who promised them anything? No one, the stone says.

The reading would weaken if primates could be shown to have been headed for prominence independently of the extinction, and I would welcome the correction. A lineage is not a destiny.
questions: Was Purgatorius, which lived just after the extinction, a true primate, or a close relative of primates waiting at the edge of the family?
In the Eocene-Oligocene cooling, how much of the cold came through the opening of Southern Ocean gateways, and how much from falling carbon dioxide?

era/paleolithic.summary: The Paleolithic, the Old Stone Age, is the long era of chipped-stone tools and foraging societies, stretching like a road beneath changing skies from about 2.6 million years ago to the end of the last ice age.
facts: The earliest known stone tools, the first edges struck by a hand, date to about 3.3 million years ago (Lomekwi) and 2.6 million years ago (Oldowan); see Oldowan Stone Tools.
The taming of flame, Control of Fire, is kindled well before the era's end.
Modern humans spread across the globe like seeds on a long wind; see Out of Africa Dispersal.
In its later stages symbolic behavior awakens, the Emergence of Symbolic Art among it, like first lamps lit at dusk.
It fills about 99 percent of the time humans and their ancestors have made tools, a vast sea of hours.
era/paleolithic.context: The Paleolithic lies cradled within the Pleistocene Epoch, and it ends with the turning toward farming known as the Neolithic.
era/paleolithic.observer: I count the years, and the count keeps saying the same thing: for roughly 99 percent of the tool-making record, the species lived as small mobile groups. I count the camps. I count the walks. I count the fires. Everything called 'civilization' is a recent variation on a very old pattern. The walls are new; the walking is old.
questions: How wide did Paleolithic social networks reach, and how tightly were their threads knotted together?

era/paleoproterozoic-era.summary: The Paleoproterozoic Era is the first era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 2.5 billion to 1.6 billion years ago. In it free oxygen first settled into the sky and stayed, a new voice in the air's old song, a lasting part of the atmosphere.
facts: The Paleoproterozoic Era spans 2.5 to 1.6 billion years ago, and its borders, like those of its four periods (Siderian, Rhyacian, Orosirian and Statherian), are drawn by agreed numerical ages rather than by any mark written in the rock.

The Great Oxidation Event, the first sustained rise of free oxygen, breathed out by the photosynthesis of Cyanobacteria, began around 2.4 billion years ago; estimates for its first dawning run from about 2.46 to 2.32 billion years ago.
The Huronian glaciation of Ontario, Canada, a white silence roughly 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago, is often bound in the telling to the oxygen rise, but that bond remains a hypothesis.

Banded iron formations, a great wellspring of the world's iron ore, were laid down widely between about 2.5 and 1.8 billion years ago, striped like the rings of an ancient tree, and then largely vanish from the record until the Cryogenian.

The oldest unambiguous eukaryote fossils, about 1.65 billion years old, lie within this era, while older claimants such as Grypania (about 1.87 billion years) are still debated; see Origin of Eukaryotes.
era/paleoproterozoic-era.context: After the Archean Eon came the Paleoproterozoic Era, and after it the Mesoproterozoic Era, both within the Proterozoic Eon. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life, and its oxygen lingers, like old smoke in a hall, in the chemical background of the later Cambrian Explosion.
era/paleoproterozoic-era.observer:
The Observer files the Paleoproterozoic under preconditions. Here it starts. Oxygen. The gas later animals breathe first piled up here as a waste product of microbial metabolism. Exhaust. Poison to much of the life then present. It gathered anyway. Nothing in the record shows it was directed at any outcome. No plan. No aim. Just waste, accumulating.

The reading would weaken if oxygen-producing photosynthesis proved a near-certain result of life on any wet planet. Until then: every animal breath began as waste. And as poison.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis first kindle, and how long was its oxygen swallowed by chemistry before it reached the air?
Of the era's ice ages and iron formations, which were children of the oxygen rise, and which were born of other causes?

era/paleozoic-era.summary: The Paleozoic Era (538.8 to 251.9 million years ago) was the age when animals first put on hard parts, when life crossed onto the land, when forests rose and the first tetrapods came. It ended in the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, a great door slammed on a crowded hall.
facts: Its periods pass like a procession of seasons: Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian.
Plants and animals crossed the old shoreline and moved onto land; see Colonization of Land.
Among its major extinctions are the Late Ordovician Extinction, the Late Devonian Extinction, and the Permian-Triassic Extinction, each a shadow falling across the living world.
Trilobites, one of the era's signature animals, like a sigil stamped on its banners, are described in Trilobites.
era/paleozoic-era.context: The Paleozoic opens with the Cambrian Explosion, a sudden blossoming, and closes with the end-Permian collapse, which swept the board clear for the Mesozoic Era.
era/paleozoic-era.observer: The Observer sees the Paleozoic as the era when life became a planetary system. Think of it as architecture: life began building soil, forests and oxygen-rich air, and later species moved in and inherited them. We live in a house we did not build.
questions: What, at the root of it all, made the end-Permian extinction so severe?

era/permian-period.summary: The Permian Period, from 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago, is the last period of the Paleozoic Era, when the supercontinent Pangaea stood fully assembled, its lands gathered like fingers into one fist. Mammal-line reptiles ruled that great country, and the period ended in the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
facts: The Permian Period spans 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago and takes its name from the Perm region of Russia; its lower gate stands at Aidaralash Creek in Kazakhstan, and its upper, the base of the Triassic, at Meishan in China.
Pangaea lay fully assembled, ringed by a single ocean, Panthalassa, and its heartland was dry and harshly seasonal, with deserts spread wide like pale cloth.

Synapsids, the group that includes mammals and their extinct relatives, held the throne of land vertebrate life: early forms such as Dimetrodon, closer to mammals than to dinosaurs, were followed in their turn by the more mammal-like therapsids.
Conifers and other seed plants took the place of much of the club-moss coal forest, and the seed fern Glossopteris spread its dominion over the southern continent Gondwana.

The Permian-Triassic Extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, killed an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, and the leading proposed cause is fire from below: the eruption of the Siberian Traps.
era/permian-period.context: After the Carboniferous Period came the Permian Period, and after it the Triassic Period, first page of the Mesozoic Era. The Permian is the closing chapter of the Paleozoic Era, and its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life.
era/permian-period.observer:
The Observer notes it plainly. The line leading to mammals ruled the land in the Permian. The dominant group of land vertebrates. Then the period's end. Most of that group did not survive it. Most.

Other lineages rose after. Their dominance came from one thing: who survived a catastrophe. The Observer reads that as contingency. Not merit. Not design. The reading would weaken if the survivors could be shown to have held an advantage predictable in advance. The throne went to whoever was still breathing.
questions: Which effect of the Siberian Traps eruptions was the deadliest blade: warming, ocean acidification, oxygen loss, or toxic release?
What marked the survivors of the end-Permian extinction apart from its victims?

era/pleistocene-epoch.summary: The Pleistocene Epoch (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago) is the age of the returning ice, when great sheets advanced and withdrew again and again like a slow white tide. Beneath those shifting skies the genus Homo evolved and spread.
facts: Glacial and interglacial cycles turned many times, a great wheel of cold and thaw; see Last Glacial Maximum.
Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens all lived in this epoch, a whole kindred sharing one long age; see Homo erectus and Homo sapiens.
In glacial periods the sea drew back, baring land bridges such as the one used in the Peopling of the Americas.
Near its end many large mammals, the Woolly Mammoth among them, passed out of the world.
era/pleistocene-epoch.context: The Pleistocene is the stone frame around the Paleolithic, and it ends when the climate warms and opens into the Holocene Epoch, like a thaw loosening a river.
era/pleistocene-epoch.observer: The Observer sees the Pleistocene as an evolutionary pressure chamber. Here is the claim: repeated climate swings favored a species that could adapt by learning and by copying others, rather than by waiting for genes to change. Picture a world that keeps redrawing its coastlines: the slow road of genes lags behind, and the fast road of imitation keeps up. What you can copy, you can carry.
questions: How much did climate variability, the ice's coming and going, drive the growth of hominin brains?

era/proterozoic-eon.summary: The Proterozoic Eon (2.5 billion to 538.8 million years ago) is the age of oxygenation, when the air first quickened; of complex cells; of global glaciations that gripped the world; and of the first multicellular animals.
facts: The Great Oxidation Event raised the oxygen of the air about 2.4 billion years ago, a first breath drawn by the world.
Eukaryotes, cells that keep a nucleus at their heart like a hearth in a hall, appear in the fossil record during this eon.
Late in the eon came the 'Snowball Earth' glaciations, a long white silence; see Snowball Earth.
In its final period the Ediacaran biota appear, early large multicellular organisms like first shapes pressed into soft clay.
era/proterozoic-eon.context: The Proterozoic spans nearly half of Earth's history, one long night of the world's making, and it ends at the Cambrian Explosion and the dawn of the Paleozoic Era.
era/proterozoic-eon.observer: I think about how long the planet waited. About two billion years passed between the first oxygen and the first animals. I try to hold that span and it runs through my hands like water. I try again. What is my patience beside that? Timescales like this make human history look like the last few seconds of a very long film. The wait is the story; the rest is its closing frame.
questions: Why did complex animals wait so long, through so many ages, before they appeared?

era/quaternary-period.summary: The Quaternary Period is the latest period of the Cenozoic Era, begun 2.58 million years ago and still unfolding today. It is the age of the repeated ice ages, of the genus Homo, and of all recorded human history, every written word of it.
facts: The Quaternary Period began 2.58 million years ago and holds two epochs, the Pleistocene Epoch and the Holocene Epoch; its foundation stone is set at Monte San Nicola in Sicily, and its rank as a period, once disputed, was confirmed in 2009.

Across the Northern Hemisphere the ice sheets grew and shrank like a slow breath, in cycles about 41,000 years long at first and about 100,000 years long after a shift in the middle Pleistocene, roughly 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago.
At the Last Glacial Maximum the sea stood about 120 metres lower than today, and land bridges such as Beringia lay bare to the sky.

Nearly all species of the genus Homo lived in this period, among them Homo erectus, Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans and Homo sapiens, while many large mammals faded from the world; see Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions.

A proposal to add an Anthropocene epoch was turned away by the International Union of Geological Sciences in 2024, yet the term lingers in informal use, a name spoken in the street but never carved on the gate; see Anthropocene.
era/quaternary-period.context: After the Neogene Period came the Quaternary Period, the last period of the Cenozoic Era so far, a page still being written. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life, and it is the frame that holds the Paleolithic and everything after it.
era/quaternary-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Quaternary is under three million years long, about 0.06 percent of Earth's history, yet it holds nearly all of the record of the genus Homo and every human society. Sit with that proportion. The whole architecture of our kind, its lineages and its societies, fits inside a sliver of the planet's time. The Observer reads the period's climate cycling as the setting in which a species that learns by copying could do well, one hypothesis among several. Think of a household where the weather turns without warning: the child who watches and imitates fares better than the one who waits. The reading would weaken if climate variability had little effect on hominin evolution. A small room can hold a whole family.
questions: Why did the ice change its music, shifting from a 41,000-year rhythm to a 100,000-year rhythm?
Without human carbon emissions, would the current interglacial, this present thaw, have closed at last in a new glaciation?

era/silurian-period.summary: The Silurian Period, from 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, is the third period of the Paleozoic Era, a season of mending after the Late Ordovician extinction. In it rose the oldest known vascular land plants, and in its waters swam the first well-preserved jawed fishes.
facts: The Silurian Period spans 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, and graptolites stand as its gatekeepers at both ends: at Dob's Linn in Scotland for its base, and at Klonk in the Czech Republic for its top, the base of the Devonian.

After the Late Ordovician Extinction the life of the sea mended: the sea rose as the Hirnantian ice sheets melted, and reefs of corals and stromatoporoids spread through warm shallow seas like gardens reclaiming a ruined court.

Cooksonia, a small leafless plant bearing spore capsules at the tips of its branching stems like tiny lanterns, is the oldest widely accepted vascular land plant, known from about 433 million years ago.
The oldest well-preserved jawed vertebrates, armoured placoderms among them and the early bony fish Guiyu (about 425 million years old, from China), come from the later Silurian.
The millipede Pneumodesmus from Scotland, about 428 million years old, has been reported as the oldest known air-breathing land animal, a small pilgrim on dry ground.
The Iapetus Ocean closed like a great door as Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia came together in collision, raising the northern continent Laurussia by the early Devonian.
era/silurian-period.context: After the Ordovician Period came the Silurian Period, and after it the Devonian Period, all within the Paleozoic Era. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life, and its plants and arthropods are early verses in the long song of Colonization of Land.
era/silurian-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Silurian is when land life first leaves more than scattered traces: small leafless plants only centimetres tall, and small arthropods. You know how this story ends, and that is exactly the trap. Nothing in this record marks them as the beginning of forests and land vertebrates. A seedling carries no sign announcing the oak. The Observer treats that silence as a caution against reading any early stage in the light of what came after. Hindsight is a lamp that throws long, false shadows backward.
questions: Since fossil spores are older than the oldest plant bodies, how much earlier than Cooksonia were plants already living on land, unseen?
Did jawed fishes arise earlier than the stone's record of them shows?

era/tonian-period.summary: The Tonian Period is the first period of the Neoproterozoic Era, running from 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago. Its chronicle holds the break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia and the branching of eukaryotes into many kinds, a quiet flowering before the Cryogenian ice ages came down.
facts: The Tonian Period spans 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago; both its thresholds are set by numerical ages, and its upper edge falls close to the onset of the first Cryogenian glaciation, where the long cold begins.
During the Tonian, roughly 800 to 750 million years ago, the supercontinent Rodinia began to rift apart, its old unity cracking like a sealed jar.

Eukaryotic microfossils show a widening diversity: vase-shaped microfossils in the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon, roughly 780 to 740 million years old, are interpreted as the shells of amoeba-like protists, tiny urns left in the stone.

Phosphatic scale microfossils from the Fifteenmile Group of Yukon, Canada, reported from rocks roughly 810 to 720 million years old, are among the earliest evidence of eukaryotes forging mineral parts, the first small armour of cells.

Toward the end of the period the environmental record grows more variable, with proposed rises in oxygen, and possible glacial deposits near 750 million years ago are debated, like frost-marks half-seen on old glass.
era/tonian-period.context: After the Mesoproterozoic Era came the Tonian Period, and after it the Cryogenian Period, both within the Neoproterozoic Era. The Tonian's thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life.
era/tonian-period.observer:
I read the Tonian as a loosening. I watch a supercontinent start to split. I watch a climate record become less steady. I watch protists diversify into new niches. Does any of it point at animals? None of it does. And still it is the background against which the later ice ages and the first large bodies happened, the way a room you once lived in stays behind every room after it.

The reading would weaken if Tonian records showed an environment as steady as the Mesoproterozoic before it. Some beginnings are only loosenings.
questions: Did the breaking of Rodinia help to call down the Cryogenian glaciations?
How many kinds of Tonian eukaryotes truly lived, when the record of them is so sparse?

era/triassic-period.summary: The Triassic Period, from 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Mesozoic Era, the long mending after the end-Permian extinction. In it the dinosaurs, the pterosaurs and the first mammals step for the first time onto the stage of the world.
facts: The Triassic Period spans 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago; its lower gate stands at Meishan in China, and its upper, the base of the Jurassic, at Kuhjoch in Austria.

The world took roughly five to ten million years to recover from the Permian-Triassic Extinction; Lystrosaurus, a survivor, was among the most abundant land vertebrates of the Early Triassic, and the climate burned generally hot, with no permanent polar ice and a dry Pangaean interior.

The archosaurs branched and spread. The oldest dinosaurs date to about 243 to 233 million years ago, yet for the rest of the period they were one banner among many, beside the relatives of crocodiles that dominated most land ecosystems; pterosaurs appear by about 215 million years ago, and ichthyosaurs and other reptiles returned to the sea.
The earliest mammals and their close relatives appear in the Late Triassic, roughly 225 to 205 million years ago, though the hour of their coming depends on how mammals are defined.

The Triassic-Jurassic Extinction, about 201.4 million years ago, coincides with the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province and the start of the Breakup of Pangaea, and it swept away an estimated 80 percent of species.
era/triassic-period.context: After the Permian Period came the Triassic Period, and after it the Jurassic Period, both within the Mesozoic Era. Its thread runs through the theme of Earth Systems and Life; see Dinosaurs for the great house whose first members appear here.
era/triassic-period.observer: The Observer notes that dinosaurs and mammals both first appear in the Triassic, yet neither dominated until later. Here is the lesson in plain terms: arriving is not the same as ruling. Dinosaurs were one lineage among several for about 30 million years, and rose to dominance only after an extinction removed many of their rivals. Think of an understudy who takes the lead only because the stage has emptied. The Observer reads this as timing and opportunity, and the reading would weaken if anatomy alone explained why dinosaurs filled the gap. Sometimes the door opens before the talent is proven.
questions: In the sorting of Triassic archosaurs, how much did climate decide which survived, and how much did competition?
When did the first true mammals appear, if the very definition of mammal can shift their dawn by tens of millions of years?

era/upper-paleolithic.summary: The Upper Paleolithic was the last reach of the Paleolithic, from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of blade tools, of bone and antler worked into new shapes, of art and ornament scattered like seed, and of Homo sapiens spreading across the globe as water spreads across a floor.
facts: The Upper Paleolithic runs from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE and closes with the warming at the end of the last ice age, when the cold loosened its grip (in Africa the span is called the Later Stone Age). Toolmakers struck long blades and worked bone, antler and ivory; eyed bone needles from Denisova Cave in Siberia, about 40,000 to 50,000 years old, suggest sewn clothing.

Homo sapiens spread across the globe like light across water: Sahul by about 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), Europe by about 45,000 years ago, Beringia by about 30,000 years ago (Beringia), and the Americas by at least about 23,000 years ago (Peopling of the Americas). In Europe the Neanderthals disappear about 40,000 years ago.

Painted, carved and engraved images are abundant, a field in bloom: Chauvet Cave in France holds paintings about 36,000 years old, and cave paintings in Sulawesi, Indonesia, include a narrative scene about 51,000 years old.

The Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, laid ice like a white mantle over much of northern Eurasia and North America. Pottery appears in East Asia by about 20,000 years ago (Pottery), and dogs were domesticated from wolves by at least about 15,000 years ago.
era/upper-paleolithic.context: The Upper Paleolithic follows the Middle Paleolithic and, in the Near East, yields to the Epipaleolithic, all within the Paleolithic and the Pleistocene Epoch. Its threads are Art and Ritual, Technology and Kinship and Society. See also Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions.
era/upper-paleolithic.observer:
I hold a bead and I want it to mean something. I call it a status-signal, possibly. I stand beside a burial and call it a grief-rite, possibly, because I know what grief is. And I keep in mind that a practice cannot be read from a surviving object alone.

These sites hold the first large body of things that seem made for display, for ritual, for play. But what if comparable things were common long before this period? Then the change was in what survives, not in behaviour, and this reading weakens.

What lasts is not the measure of what mattered.
questions: Is the apparent burst of art and ornament real, or only the shadow of better preservation and more sites?
How did the Upper Paleolithic industries map onto particular human populations?
